title: BEFORE HE COULD TOUCH HER, GOD MADE HIM WAIT
paragraphs: BEFORE HE COULD TOUCH HER, GOD MADE HIM WAIT

A captive woman had lost her home, perhaps her family, and almost everything familiar to her. Then, in a brutal world where victorious men possessed extraordinary power over defeated women, God put something between a soldier’s desire and this grieving captive: time. Deuteronomy 21:10–14 is uncomfortable. It should be. But hidden inside this difficult law is a truth about the character of God that becomes breathtaking when we finally see where the whole biblical story is going.
Imagine her.
Not as a theological problem.
Not as a verse you are trying to defend.
As a woman.
The battle is over.
Smoke hangs over what used to be home.
The voices she knew are disappearing behind her.
She does not know what tomorrow looks like.
She does not know whether the people she loves are alive.
She does not know whether she will ever see her homeland again.
And now she is a captive.
Then an Israelite soldier sees her.
Scripture does not romanticize what happens next.
It says:
"וְרָאִיתָ בַּשִּׁבְיָה אֵשֶׁת יְפַת־תֹּאַר וְחָשַׁקְתָּ בָהּ"
Vera'ita bashivyah eshet yefat-to'ar, vechashaqta vah...

“You see among the captives a beautiful woman, and you desire her...”
—Deuteronomy 21:11
That Hebrew word is important.
וְחָשַׁקְתָּ — vechashaqta.
You desire her.
The text begins with the desire of the powerful man.
But then something happens.
He does not simply get everything his desire wants immediately.
God interrupts him.
The woman is brought into the household, and the text describes her tending to her hair and nails, removing the clothing of her captivity, remaining in the house...
and grieving.
Listen to the Hebrew:
"וּבָכְתָה אֶת־אָבִיהָ וְאֶת־אִמָּהּ יֶרַח יָמִים"
Uvakhtah et-aviha ve'et-immah yerach yamim.
“And she shall weep for her father and her mother a month of days.”
A month.
Thirty days, approximately, depending upon the lunar month.
Before the relationship described by the law could proceed, her grief occupied the house.
Think about that.
The victorious soldier had power.
He had desire.
He had opportunity.
But desire was not allowed to erase mourning.
For an entire month, this woman’s tears became part of his world.
He would know she was crying.
He would know she had a father.
He would know she had a mother.
He would know that the woman he found beautiful was also somebody’s daughter.
That matters.
And yet we must be careful here.
We should not turn Deuteronomy 21 into something sentimental that it is not.
This woman was still a captive.
There was an enormous imbalance of power.
The passage does not describe modern courtship between two free people meeting on equal terms, and Christians should not pretend otherwise.
Nor should we use this passage to justify sexual coercion, wartime abuse, trafficking, forced marriage, or the exploitation of vulnerable women.
The law addresses an ancient wartime reality and places restrictions upon the victorious Israelite man within that reality.
The text makes him wait.
The text acknowledges her mourning.
The text moves the relationship into the category of wife rather than disposable sexual property.
And the following verse adds another startling restriction.
If the man later ceases to want her, Scripture says:
Veshillachtah lenafshah.
He must let her go free.
Then comes the prohibition:
"וּמָכֹר לֹא־תִמְכְּרֶנָּה בַּכָּסֶף"
Umachor lo-timkerennah bakasef.
“You shall certainly not sell her for money.”
He could not decide:
I don't want her anymore, so perhaps I can make money from her.
No.
She was not merchandise.
She could not simply be converted into cash.
The man who once saw a beautiful captive was being forced to confront something lust and power constantly try to forget:
she was a human being.
And suddenly this ancient passage becomes painfully modern.
Because we still live in a world that sees people before it knows people.
We see a beautiful body before we see a wounded soul.
We see somebody’s usefulness before we see their humanity.
We swipe.
Scroll.
Desire.
Consume.
Discard.
Sometimes we do it sexually.
Sometimes emotionally.
Sometimes financially.
Sometimes even spiritually.
We can become so accustomed to asking, “What can this person give me?” that we forget to ask, “What has this person survived?”
Maybe that is where this passage finds you.
Because perhaps you have been the person who desired without understanding.
Or perhaps...
you have been the person nobody bothered to understand.
Maybe somebody loved your appearance but never learned your pain.
Maybe somebody wanted your body but had no interest in your tears.
Maybe somebody enjoyed what you could provide until providing became difficult.
Maybe somebody promised permanence and treated you as disposable.
Maybe you were abandoned when you were no longer convenient.
And somewhere inside you there is still a person mourning what was taken.
A childhood.
A marriage.
A parent.
A relationship.
Trust.
Safety.
Innocence.
Years you cannot recover.
Perhaps everyone around you thinks you should have moved on by now.
But God knows grief cannot always be commanded to disappear.
There is something astonishing about those words:
"וּבָכְתָה... יֶרַח יָמִים"
She shall weep... a month of days.
Scripture makes room for tears.
Not because thirty days magically cures grief.
It doesn't.
But because biblical faith is not built upon pretending pain never happened.
God repeatedly encounters people in Scripture inside their sorrow.
Hagar cries in the wilderness.
Hannah weeps before the Lord.
David drenches his bed with tears.
Jeremiah becomes known as the weeping prophet.
Jesus Himself stands before Lazarus' tomb and weeps.
The shortest verse many Christians memorized as children contains one of Christianity's deepest revelations:
“Jesus wept.”
The Son of God did not consider tears beneath holiness.
And that changes the way we read this captive woman's month.
Her grief was not an inconvenience to be edited out of the story.
She was allowed to mourn.
Somebody reading this needs permission to hear that.
You can love Jesus and still cry.
You can trust God and still miss somebody.
You can believe in resurrection and still ache beside a grave.
You can forgive and still need healing.
You can worship while carrying questions you cannot answer.
Faith is not the absence of grief.
Sometimes faith is bringing your grief into the presence of God instead of allowing grief to drive you away from Him.
But there is an even deeper confrontation waiting inside this passage.
The law restrains what a powerful person may do to someone vulnerable.
That pattern matters profoundly for followers of Jesus.
Because the Gospel does not teach us to ask how much power we are permitted to exercise over another person.
Jesus teaches us what love does with power.
Look at Christ.
The One possessing all authority does not exploit the weak.
He receives them.
He touches lepers others avoided.
He welcomes children others considered interruptions.
He speaks publicly with women others dismissed.
He eats with sinners religious society despised.
He sees the overlooked.
He restores the disgraced.
He defends the vulnerable.
And then the One with all authority does something almost incomprehensible.
He kneels.
He washes feet.
Then He goes to a cross.
The Gospel turns the world's understanding of power upside down.
Human sin says:
I have power, therefore I can take.
Jesus says:
I have power, therefore I can serve.
Human lust says:
I desire you, therefore you owe me.
Christlike love says:
I love you, therefore I seek your good.
Human cruelty says:
You are no longer useful, therefore you are disposable.
The Gospel announces:
You bear the image of God, therefore you possess a dignity your usefulness never created and your weakness cannot erase.
This is why Christianity can never use Deuteronomy 21 to excuse abuse.
The Bible's story is moving somewhere.
Toward Jesus Christ.
Toward the King who refuses to treat broken people like conquered property.
Toward the Bridegroom who gives Himself for His bride.
Toward the Savior who does not purchase us in order to exploit us but gives His own blood to redeem us from slavery to sin.
And there is an uncomfortable question waiting for every one of us.
Have you been treating people as people...
or as things?
Your spouse.
Your boyfriend.
Your girlfriend.
Your employees.
Your children.
Your parents.
The attractive stranger on your screen.
The person whose body became entertainment.
The person whose weakness became gossip.
The person whose scandal became content.
The person you stopped calling when they stopped benefiting you.
Christianity is not merely about avoiding obvious cruelty.
Jesus goes after the heart.
The same human heart capable of turning another person into an object is the heart Christ came to transform.
And that means this story cannot end with us pointing at an ancient soldier.
Eventually the finger turns around.
Toward us.
What has your desire made you justify?
What has your anger made you dehumanize?
Who became disposable when they disappointed you?
Whose tears did you ignore because their pain interrupted what you wanted?
Those are difficult questions.
But grace does not become beautiful until sin becomes honest.
The Gospel does not say, “Pretend you never sinned.”
The Gospel says:
Repent.
Turn around.
Bring the ugliness into the light.
Because Jesus Christ did not die for the imaginary version of you who never failed.
He died for sinners.
That is the scandal.
And that is the grace.
At the cross, humanity did the unthinkable.
We rejected the Holy One.
Mocked the innocent One.
Stripped Him.
Humiliated Him.
Nailed Him to wood.
And Jesus answered human sin with an offer of mercy.
Not cheap mercy.
Blood-bought mercy.
The cross does not tell us sin does not matter.
The cross tells us sin mattered enough that redemption cost Christ His life.
And resurrection tells us sin does not get the final sentence.
That is why your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
The adulterer can repent.
The porn addict can repent.
The abusive person can repent and must stop abusing.
The bitter person can repent.
The manipulator can repent.
The person drowning in shame can come home.
The wounded can begin healing.
The guilty can be forgiven.
The captive can become free.
Not because evil suddenly becomes acceptable.
Because Jesus Christ rewrites human lives through repentance, forgiveness, redemption, and transforming grace.
Maybe this article exposed something you have kept hidden.
Don't perform spirituality here.
Be honest.
Someone reading those words may realize they are not the only person fighting their way back toward the light.
That is what Christian community should do.
Not celebrate sin.
Not weaponize shame.
Lead one another toward Jesus.
Send this privately to someone who has been treated as disposable.
Grace cannot be purchased.
But voluntary generosity can glorify God when it flows from a willing heart and is used faithfully for Gospel work.
Pray.
Tell another wounded person where you found encouragement.
Because somewhere tonight there may be another person sitting alone with a phone glowing in a dark room, believing the lie that what happened to them made them worthless.
Maybe your tag interrupts the worst night of their year.
And maybe a difficult law about an unnamed captive woman becomes the doorway through which they encounter something they desperately needed to remember:
God sees human beings where sinful people see objects.
God hears mourning others find inconvenient.
And Jesus receives sinners whom shame tells to stay away.
That woman in Deuteronomy 21 is never given a name.
We don't know what her voice sounded like.
We don't know what memories made her cry hardest during that month.
We don't know what happened every night when the house became quiet and memories returned.
But Scripture did not erase her tears.
Thousands of years later...
we are still reading about them.
Perhaps that is the line you need to carry with you tonight.

What the world tried to reduce to someone's possession, Scripture still forces us to remember as someone's daughter—and what sin has tried to reduce to your worst chapter, Jesus can still redeem into a testimony of grace.
Bring Him the scandal.
Bring Him the grief.
Bring Him the hidden thing.
Bring Him the years you wish you could recover.
Bring Him the sin you cannot excuse.
Bring Him the wound you cannot erase.
Come honestly.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Forgive as Christ teaches you to forgive.
Seek safety where abuse exists.
Make restitution where you have harmed others.
Receive mercy where shame has convinced you mercy is impossible.
And keep your eyes on Jesus.
Because the deepest message of Scripture is not that human beings never make ruins of things.
We do.
The message is that ruins do not frighten the Redeemer.
Your tears may belong to a chapter you never would have chosen—but they do not get to write the last sentence when the pen is surrendered to Jesus.
